linkedin.about:
Simon Sinek is an unshakable optimist who believes in a bright future and our ability to build it together. Simon's WHY is to inspire people to do what inspires them so that, together, each of us can change our world for the better.

With a vision to change the way businesses think, act, and operate, Simon and his team work with leaders and organizations in nearly every industry to help transform company culture and create a better working world.

As a trained ethnographer, Simon has discovered remarkable patterns about how the greatest leaders and organizations think, act, and communicate. He is fascinated by the people and organizations that make the greatest, lasting impact on the world. He has devoted his life to sharing his thinking, and leading a movement to inspire people to do the things that inspire them.

Simon may be best known for popularizing the concept of WHY in his first Ted Talk in 2009. It has since become one of the most watched talks of all time on TED.com, with 37+ million views. 

Simon is a bestselling author and shares his ideas in the books Start With Why, Leaders Eat Last, Together Is Better, Find Your Why, and The Infinite Game.

Learn more at simonsinek.com.

analysis.summary: Simon is a self-described unshakable optimist whose whole public life is organized around one question: how do people feel inspired, safe and fulfilled? He is a teacher and conversationalist at heart, happiest on a stage, in an armchair with a mic, or in a long talk with a thoughtful guest. His feed is almost entirely ideas about vulnerability, honest friendship, legacy and the value of struggle, so the person outside work shows up mainly as someone who thinks hard about how humans connect. His bio hints at a wish to experience as much of life as possible (run, jump, laugh, cry, love, hope).
analysis.tagline: Unshakable optimist looking for someone honest enough to tell me what I need to hear.

needs.label: Honest truth-teller
needs.detail: He needs a partner who cares enough to be candid rather than just agreeable.
needs.evidence: "The people who help us grow are the ones who care enough to be honest with us. Who's the person in your life who always tells you the…"

needs.label: Real vulnerability
needs.detail: He needs a partner who reaches out directly when they are struggling and welcomes him doing the same.
needs.evidence: Quote graphic: "Vulnerability happens when we're feeling vulnerable and we reach out to someone."

needs.label: Shared purpose
needs.detail: He needs a partner who finds meaning in contribution and understands that his mission is central to his life.
needs.evidence: LinkedIn: "inspire people to do what inspires them"; IG bio: "to experience as much as I can for one purpose: to inspire."

needs.label: Growth through struggle
needs.detail: He needs someone who doesn't shortcut difficulty and will work through hard things together.
needs.evidence: "The struggle is the point. The process of figuring things out is what teaches us, fulfills us and, in the end, makes us happy."

needs.label: Asking for help freely
needs.detail: He needs a relationship where asking for support is normal and quick.
needs.evidence: Tells the story of friend Maria Shriver: asking "Do you have 8 minutes?" when we need help is "one of the most powerful practices."

needs.evidence: Book "Together Is Better"; "believe in this bright future and our ability to build it together."

personality.description: He is intellectually curious and expressive, constantly synthesizing ideas from guests like Arthur Brooks and comfortable on stage with animated gestures, which suggests high openness and extraversion. His steady optimism and prolific, consistent output (books, podcast, imprint, nonprofit) suggest calm stability and discipline, though only public-facing material is visible.

loveLanguage.why: His content centers on being present, asking for 8 minutes of someone's time, honest friends, and long talks; connection through attentive dialogue is the clearest pattern.

analysis.idealPartner: Someone warm, candid and emotionally brave, who tells him the truth kindly and reaches out when they are struggling. They would share his sense of purpose, enjoy big conversations about meaning, and see partnership as a team where together is better.

linkedin.about:
Mel Robbins is the creator and host of the award-winning The Mel Robbins Podcast, one of the most successful podcasts in the world, and a #1 New York Times bestselling author of The Let Them Theory. She's also the founder and CEO of the media production company 143 Studios. She has amassed 40 million followers online and is one of the most respected experts in mindset, life improvement, and behavior change. The Wall Street Journal calls her a “billion-view podcaster” and TIME Magazine says she gives millions of listeners around the globe “a reason to believe in themselves.”

Her books have been translated into 63 languages and include the #1 New York Times, #1 Amazon, #1 Audible, and #1 Sunday Times bestselling The Let Them Theory, which is the top selling book of 2025 according to Publisher’s Weekly, with 7 million copies sold within nine months of its release date. It is on pace to have the best non-fiction book launch of all time. She is also the author of the multimillion-copy-selling The 5 Second Rule, The High 5 Habit, and seven #1 audiobook releases on Audible.

USA Today calls Mel “a force to be reckoned with.” She is a global phenomenon in the publishing industry and podcasting. Her Boston-based media production company, 143 Studios, produces award-winning content, podcasts, events, audio series, online courses, journals, and books, along with professional development education forpartners likeStarbucks, Ulta Beauty, JP Morgan Chase, LinkedIn, Headspace, and Audible.

The Mel Robbins Podcast has won some of the most prestigious awards given to podcasts, including Webby, Signal Awards, and iHeart. It was also recognized as one of Apple Podcasts' Top Shared and Followed Shows of 2024 and 2023 and Spotify Top Global Shows of 2024. Notable accolades for Robbins include being named to Time 100 Most Influential Digital Voices of 2025, a Forbes 50 Over 50 Honoree, USA Today Top 5 Mindset & Performance Coaches in the World, and one of the fifty most influential influencers on The Hollywood Reporter’s Creator A-List in 2024.

Thanks for being here!

He treats self-improvement as a shared, joyful project, recommending dating books, reading widely, and framing life as something you design backwards from the lifestyle you want. He comes across as warm, relentlessly curious and a little nerdy, with a big open grin in almost every photo.

linkedin.about:
Gary Vaynerchuk is a serial entrepreneur and serves as the Chairman of VaynerX, the CEO of VaynerMedia, and Creator and CEO of VeeFriends, and 6x New York Times Best Selling Author. Gary is considered one of the leading global minds on what's next in culture, business, and the internet.   

Known as "GaryVee," he is described as one of the most forward thinkers in business. He acutely recognizes trends and patterns early to help others understand how shifts in consumer attention impact the realities of the business world today. Gary's approach sits at the intersection of business and pop culture. He keenly understands how to bring brand relevance to the forefront. He is a prolific angel investor with early investments in companies like Facebook, Twitter, Tumblr, Venmo, Snapchat, Coinbase, and Uber.    

Gary is an entrepreneur at heart – he builds businesses. Today, he helps Fortune 1000 brands leverage consumer attention through his full-service advertising agency, VaynerMedia, which has ofﬁces in Amsterdam, Bangkok, Chicago, Delhi, Kuala Lumpur, London, Los Angeles, Mexico City, Miami, New York, Tokyo, Toronto, Singapore, and Sydney. VaynerMedia is part of the VaynerX modern-day parent company, which also includes Eva Nosidam Productions, Gallery Media Group, ChukMedia, VaynerSpeakers, VaynerCommerce, Tamara Group, and Tingley Lane Trading. Gary is the Co-Founder of VaynerSports, VCR Group, VaynerWatt, Resy, and Empathy Wines. He guided Resy and Empathy to successful exits -- which he later sold to American Express and Constellation Brands, respectively. He also owns a Major League Pickleball team called the 5s, is part owner of a Big3 basketball team, and is an investor in the revival of the SlamBall League.   

Gary is also the founder and creator of VeeCon – a contemporary super conference that converges business and pop culture with innovation and technology. In addition to running multiple businesses, Gary documents his daily life as a CEO through his social media channels, which have more than 50 million followers and garner more than 2+ billion impressions per year across all platforms. His podcast, "The GaryVee Audio Experience," ranks among the top podcasts globally.    

Gary serves on the board of MikMak, Bojangles Restaurants, Global Citizen Forum, The Paley Center, and Pencils of Promise. He is also an advisor for District and a longtime Well Member of charity: water.  

Gary's life ambition is to buy the New York Jets.

analysis.summary: Adam Grant is a professional curiosity machine: a Wharton psychologist who turns research into plain-language insight and then actually practices it, from tough-love mentoring to quality-of-attention in relationships. Outside the lecture hall he is playful and physical. He climbed back onto a diving board after years away, flips on a backyard trampoline holding his own book, and happily embarrasses his teenagers. He is warmly earnest and openly opinionated about fairness and decency, and he credits and amplifies other thinkers constantly.

posts.caption:
Four ways to change human behavior:

To get them to DO something:
1) Give them a cookie (add +)
2) Dont have to do chores (minus -)

To get them to STOP doing:
1) Make them do chores (add -) 
2) Stop giving them cookies 
(remove +)

And reinforce new behavior with urgency.
“I need to apologize Alex”

Hiring talented people is one of the easiest 10x-100x ROI opportunities.

And there’s always underpriced talent.

No one cares about what you’ve done. 
They care about what you can do for them.
Price is what you pay. Value is what you get. Which means great value can still be a bad deal.

For all the talk of enterprise value and multiples, friendly reminder that it’s okay to just make money now. Sell some “unscalable” stuff for way more than it costs. Pocket the difference. Live your life.
Rather than buying things for less than their worth, make your brand so strong that when you buy something, it becomes more valuable by its association to you.

Pricing is the single strongest lever on profit in a business.

And yet - 95% of business owners look at what everyone else is charging, take the average, make that their price and never think about it again.

The problem is - the business owners they’re copying are broke too.

You want to sleep at night like you know everything is gonna work out.

And you want to wake up like there’s no chance it’ll happen unless you take relentless, unyielding, like-your-life-depends-on-it action.

If you’re not making money, it’s because:

You don’t know how to solve a valuable problem.
Or 
You can but no one knows about you.

That’s it.

linkedin.about:
Randi Zuckerberg has long been a pioneer in both technology & media. As an early employee at Facebook & the creator of Facebook Live, she was on the front lines of shaping the social internet & how billions interact with content. Her lifelong passion for the arts paired with her tech career has been pivotal in her quest to help families navigate the complexities of an increasingly digital landscape.

Now, her unique skillset is more valuable than ever as these worlds collide with the emergence of AI & blockchain. As both an early adopter & prominent voice for women in crypto-adoption, Randi knows firsthand that these disruptive technologies offer unparalleled opportunities for autonomy, ownership, & financial success to creators and consumers alike. 

In response to the crypto market’s growing gap in diversity, inclusion, & accessibility, Randi founded HUG in early 2022 with the mission of empowering artists to become successful creative entrepreneurs. HUG is an inclusive social platform that democratizes access to the arts by providing creators with tooling to showcase & sell both physical & digital work, while also connecting them with one another & one-of-a-kind opportunities for their art.

As of 2024, Randi’s leadership has led HUG to become a global community of more than 35,000 artists from 170 countries & counting, with Randi having personally mentored over a thousand of them with their crypto-enabled businesses. HUG continues to support artists through its three core tenets of discovery, opportunity, & education, & has to date placed thousands of independent artists into their first exhibitions around the world. HUG has also distributed over $300,000 in grants & scholarships directly to independent creators, & continues to partner with entities such as L'Oréal, Mastercard, Forbes, Christie's, MoMA, the United Nations, & more in support of artists & creative technologists. 

Randi holds a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology from Harvard University. She serves as both an investor & advisor to several early & mid-stage companies and sits on the board of directors for The Motley Fool & Life360.

Alongside her career as a tech innovator, she is an accomplished artist & producer who has performed on Broadway, winning three Tony awards. She hosts a weekly business talk radio show, Randi Zuckerberg Means Business, on SiriusXM. She is an avid runner, having completed several ultra-marathons with podium finishes. While she may be known as “Mom to Start-ups”, Randi spends her days learning, growing, & sharing her love for arts with her husband and children.

posts.caption:
✨🦄 NEW PR AT THE BOSTON MARATHON!!! 🦄✨

3:27:37
7:55/mile pace
Four minute PR from my best previous time at Berlin 2024

Honestly, still speechless over this. I cannot believe that at age 44, one week after a 100k race, five months post-injury…that this happened. An entire marathon at a mile pace that starts with a 7! A Boston Qualifying time AT BOSTON! And to do this with my son here with me! OMFG!!! 

Have been working so so hard, and it doesn’t always come together on race day. But when it does…there’s no feeling quite like it. 

Time to go eat all the food and cry so many happy tears.

Fastest Known Time on the Baja Sur 135km Trail! 

On March 6, I attempted the Fastest Known Time (FKT) for Mexico’s 135km Baja Sur Trail across the entire Baja Sur Peninsula. 

82 miles from the Pacific Ocean → Sea of Cortez.
13,000 feet of elevation.
One absolutely savage mountain section from miles 17–34 that climbed 6,000 feet in just 6 miles — including three straight miles at 30% grade in peak heat.
40 miles through night under the moon and stars.
One 5-minute dirt nap after mile 60.
And a sunrise at mile 70 that made the entire effort feel almost spiritual.

My first “comeback” ultra di…

Officially a @cocodona250 finisher.
Still processing the experience and will have a more in depth post soon, but for now: 

257 miles across Arizona
36,000+ feet of elevation
6 total hours of sleep across 5 days
Torrential rain, insane heat, snow, lightning & hail
Insane amounts of Coca Cola & cookies consumed
65 miles done on a busted shin/ankle
Hysterical laugher and full body crying 
Met my own soul (several times)
Literally the greatest friends on the planet
An accomplishment nobody can ever take from me

📷: @howiesternphoto @ekzooks

Episode 262 for 26.2 miles of Chicago! 

Did Chicago live up to the hype that @sixstar_erika gives it? Find out with some incredible special guest to jumped on for a group chat style talk about their weekend experience. 

Thank you to @coachwatt_ @marathonpandamaurice and @randizuckerberg for joining us again🏃‍♀️🏃‍♂️ 🏃‍♀️🩵

Congratulations to all the #chicagomarathon finishers! 

Listen or watch this episode everywhere you get podcasts!

My ginormous baby is TWELVE today!!! 🥹🎂❤️

We are celebrating with a mother-son adventure in Chicago! A weekend of running, matching outfits, deep dish pizza, friends and birthday surprises. 

Happy birthday, Simi! I love watching you grow up, even if I wish you’d slow down just a tiny bit. (Vertically and literally)

We are officially an entire running family now. 

Today’s family scoreboard at the Run For Love 5k:

🏆 Asher WON THE ENTIRE RACE! 

🔥 Shira broke 10 MINUTES in the mile!!! 
Tiny legs, enormous swagger.

🏃 Simi casually knocked out 5 miles BEFORE the 5k for an 8-mile long run as training for his half marathon

🥉 Mom took 3rd overall female in the 5K, desperately clinging to relevance as Asher smoked her

❤️ Dad paced Simi to glory for his entire 8 mile run and coached Shira with a last minute pep talk at the start line. 

PRs. Podiums. Long runs. Matching outfits. Donuts. 

I fear I have c…

Miami 100 mile ultra.
First place female and second fastest female time ever!

Miami, you were beautiful, painful, chaotic, insane and amazing in all the best ways. The race was an adventure-style checkpoint race, where you didn’t learn the course until you were in it, and you got the directions for each checkpoint in real time. I ran over bridges, around islands, through neighborhoods, and navigated crowded touristy areas. All in hot and crazy humid Florida weather. 

When @joecorcione said he thought I was capable of running a ~20 hour 100 miler time (roughly a 12 minute mile, including sto…

The past few days have seen some fun milestones!!

🍊 My 1,000th OrangeTheory class! 
I walked into OTF almost four years ago with no clue how that gym would change my life. Countless 6am classes, some of my closest friendships, big goals dreamt & done, and a whole lot of life lived under those orange lights. Naturally, we celebrated the only reasonable way: a 6am toga party. 

🔥 My son’s new 5k PR! I got to run side by side in matching outfits with my son Simi, as he dug so deep and set a new PR on the exact same course where he last set a PR at this distance, two years ago. Super proud mom…

Apparently tapering for a race doesn’t HAVE to be a disaster. (Who knew?)

This week included: 70 miles, an actual full rest day (!!) and a truly unreasonable amount of fun:

👫 Doubles HYROX with my husband — we crushed our goals and had an absolute blast. Thank goodness for his ability to pull a sled and let me passenger princess that one…

🏃‍♀️ A long run to visit a friend, because apparently I now make house calls by foot

🏃‍♂️ Intervals with rock star friend + pacer Ben, who for some reason, continues to voluntarily participate in my nonsense

😂 An “apology tour” park loop — because d…

93 miles this week in the most unhinged, fun, “Randi” way ever

🏃‍♀️ Monday: A new 50K PR in a time trial with @dr.joelipsky biking alongside me for all 31.1 miles
🌙 Thursday (Weds night?): An all-out 1-mile race through Times Square at 1AM with my son 
@orchardstreetrunners absolutely epic OSR1
🎥: Also Thursday: Live taping of a Peloton tread class with @mattwilpers 
💪 Friday: A solo HYROX with @sydneysmith812 — and my husband cheering. And then getting to cheer for him! 
🏅 Sunday: Carderock Trail Half Marathon in 1:45:43 — 4th place woman, 1st in my age group!
Thanks @bishopseventsllc …

Normal mother-son activities: dinner, movies, a board game

Us: racing one mile at 1am through Times Square 🏃‍♀️🏃‍♂️

Do I have a mini me or what?! 😂 

Some families make memories during normal waking hours. We are not those families. 

Thanks @orchardstreetrunners for the awesome vibes and great memories. 

Side note: Both Asher and I got PRs in the mile! Asher ran a 5:05 and I ran a 6:24!

I’ve been thinking a LOT about pressure lately.

The pressure to perform. To lead. To win. To keep going when things get hard. And, as someone who thinks running 100 miles is a reasonable recreational activity 😂, I’m endlessly fascinated by the question:

What makes some people extraordinarily good under pressure?

I’m SO excited to share that after twelve years of my business talk radio show on SiriusXM, our show is back better than ever for our thirteenth year with a whole new relaunch:

🎙️ UNDER PRESSURE with Randi Zuckerberg

I’ll be sitting down with some of the mentally toughest peopl…

posts.caption:
Some words stick with you.

Over the years, I’ve collected a few quotes that genuinely changed the way I think, work, and move through life. 💭

These are a few I still come back to, because sometimes the right words at the right time can change everything.

Swipe through, and tell me: which one do you need to hear right now? 👇

Sometimes the voice telling you to quit is wisdom. Sometimes it’s fear, doubt, exhaustion, or the discomfort of doing something that actually matters. 💭

The trick is learning to tell the difference.

Before you give up, pause. Get curious. Ask yourself what’s really going on—and what you actually want.

What's something you quit that turned out to be a blessing? Tell me in the comments. 👇

Throwing it back to my conversation with Lewis Howes. 

There’s a big difference between easy money and making money easy. 💰

In my conversation with Lewis Howes, we talked about the temptation to chase the shortcut—the next big opportunity, the get-rich-quick promise, the thing that looks like easy money.

But “easy money” can come with a very expensive lesson.

Making money easy is different. It’s about building the skills, experience, and systems that make creating wealth more sustainable over time.

Want to hear the full conversation with Lewis? Comment MONEY and I’ll send you the episod…

Quick question: How many sales might you have lost when the right person landed on your website, opened your email, or saw your post…
…but your words didn’t click? 😬

Great copy isn’t about sounding clever, polished, or “professional.”
It’s about knowing how to write words that connect, persuade, and sound unmistakably like YOU.

Because in a noisy world,  writing that connects is a SUPER POWER.
And the good news? It’s a skill you can learn. 🙌

I created a FREE 7-Day Writing Class to help you do exactly that.
Comment WRITE and I’ll send it your way. 💌

And P.S. — if you’re ready to go much…

posts.caption: Everybody is jealous of the destination. Nobody is jealous of the journey.

5 money rules my wife and I follow as a couple aged 45 with two kids.

1. We don’t spend money to look rich. 

We spend to become wealthy and gain freedom of our time.

So, there’s no car. It’s rented. 
We own the house we live in, no other real estate.

No spending on brands. No spending just to show off to people.

2. We spend extravagantly on high-quality food.

We know that what goes into our body is ultimately the biggest wealth we have, and unfortunately, healthy food is not cheap.

3. We spend on experiences more than things.

Things give you happiness once, and they have no end.

You …

Before you say yes to marriage, check these 5 things.

1. Why are you getting married? Is it for the sake of society? Is it for the sake of your parents? Is it for your own good?

2. How do you handle fights with your partner? Because fights will continue. If you handle them properly, then relationships will progress.

3. Do you have an alignment on money and responsibility? How will you spend money? How will you share responsibilities?

4. Do you have space for your own personality? You can make friends without involving their friends. You can live your own life without depending on them.

5…

We overcomplicate self-improvement.

We wait for the big change, the perfect plan, the dramatic turnaround.

But most of life gets better through small rules, followed again and again.

Wait 30 days. 
Do the 2-minute task now. 
Never shrink yourself for a relationship.

Start with one this week.

4 signs that your life is much better than you think.

1/ Someone in your family has stopped worrying about you - because they trust you now.

2/ Your 18-year-old self wouldn't believe where you've reached.

3/ People now ask you for advice about something you once used to panic about.

4/ One bad day doesn't ruin your entire week, one bad week doesn't ruin your month, and one bad month doesn't ruin your year.

Sometimes, you've already made more progress than you realise.

There's a difference we often miss.

Being dependent means you need them to function. 
Being dependable means they can count on you, and you on them, without either of you losing yourselves.

One comes from fear. 
The other comes from strength.

The strongest relationships aren't two people who can't live without each other.

They're two whole people who choose, every day, to be someone the other can rely on.

3 reasons we bought our first home at 40 and not at 25 or 30.

1/ By the time we hit 40, we knew we wanted to live in Delhi.

At 25 or 30, there’s so much flexibility in life to change cities, even change countries if you want to.

But by the time we reached 40, we already knew we’re going to stay here. That’s why we chose this place.

2/ At that time, we had enough money that we could afford its EMI and its down payment for the house we wanted to live in.

At 25 or 30, that house wasn’t affordable for us.

3/ The house we wanted to live in is a very premium apartment.

The locality we wanted…

Raunak spent years struggling to get his words out.

Today, he helps others find their voice. 

A story of resilience, transformation and finding strength in his own voice 💪

Should you tell your parents how much you earn?

There’s a case for yes. They raised you, supported you, and may have every reason to know.

But there’s another side.

Once they know your salary, expectations can change - a bigger house, a car, a trip, a higher contribution at home.

So instead of telling them exactly how much you earn, you could tell them what your money can do for them.

“I can contribute ₹X towards the house.”

“I can afford this trip.”

“I can cover this EMI.”

Tell them what your money can do, not necessarily how much you make.

A counterpoint of view - do you agree?

Some people don't add to your life. 
They slowly drain it.

The ones who confuse you. 
The ones who hurt you and call it a joke. 
The ones who take your energy and give nothing back.

We keep them around out of guilt, or history, or habit.

But protecting your peace isn't cold. 
It's necessary.

You're allowed to walk away from anyone who only knows how to take.

5 questions people ask - and how we hear them.

1/ “When are you getting married?”

We hear that nothing I’ve done in life so far means nothing until I get married.

2/ “How much do you earn now?”

We hear that my entire worth is based on one salary, one number, and that will give me a rank.

3/ “Sharma ji’s son, well…”

We hear that I will never be enough. Someone else will always be doing better than me.

4/ “You studied so much and you’re doing this?”

We hear that if I make my own choices in life, that will never be accepted.

5/ “You’ve gotten a little healthy.”

When a child is punished for the truth, they don’t stop doing the thing.

They just get better at hiding it.

Fear doesn’t build honesty. 
It builds distance. 
It teaches a child that the safest option is to never let you see who they really are.

The kids who grow up telling their parents the truth aren’t the ones who were scared into it.They’re the ones who knew the truth was safe.

posts.caption:
We started with a baby in one arm and a startup idea in the other. 👶🏼 🧑🏻‍💻 👩🏻‍💻 

The journey from 1 brand to 7 (and an IPO in between!) wasn’t a straight line, it was a series of ups, downs, and COVID-sized hurdles.

If you’re feeling the fear today, remember: we were terrified too. 

Here’s to the dreamers, the “banned” builders, and the 1,000 moms who helped us find our way. 🥂

[2016 trend, 2026, nostalgia, startups]

Inki mehnat aur success ki story hai sabse alag.
Ghazal Alagh ne Weekend Ka Vaar ko diya motivation aur fun ka perfect mix. Aapne dekha?

Dekhiye #BiggBoss19 ka naya episode, har roz raat 9 baje #JioHotstar par aur 10:30 baje @colorstv par.

#BiggBossOnJioHotstar #BB19OnJioHotstar

@beingsalmankhan @ghazalalagh @gauravkhannaofficial @tanyamittalofficial @ashnoorkaur @iam_kunickaasadanand @rj_pranit @farrhana_bhatt @amaal_mallik @badeshashehbaz @maltichahar
A surreal feeling 🥰

From the archives when we sat, expressed and observed the evening change colours 🌇

Wine kept up with us 🍷

I went to almost 10 dermatologists when I was struggling with severe hormonal acne.

And every time, I came back with another expensive prescription.

One day I randomly flipped one of the bottles and started reading what was actually inside it.

2% Salicylic Acid.
10% Niacinamide.

And I remember thinking, why are these ingredients so expensive? Why can’t people just get effective formulations at prices that actually make sense?

That thought stayed with me.

And eventually, it became the idea behind The Derma Co. and Aqualogica.

The goal was pretty simple. Be transparent about what goes in…

Not all men are the problem. But the ones who are, need to be held accountable.

But for those who choose to hurt women, is protest enough?
When does outrage turn into action?

Women shouldn’t have to live wondering, “Could I be next?”

Let’s demand accountability.
Let’s demand change.
And let’s make sure the right people face the consequences.
It’s only love and love is all I have ❤️

My mornings don’t change much. Same quiet 30 minutes before anyone needs anything from me. Same handful of decisions I don’t have to think about — what I eat, when I move, when the laptop opens and when it shuts. None of it photographs well. None of it would make an interesting reel on its own.

But here’s what I’ve noticed — the days that go well aren’t the days something exciting happens. They’re the days the boring stuff already happened, so I have the bandwidth left for whatever actually needs my full attention. A predictable routine isn’t the opposite of ambition. It’s what makes ambitio…

When my husband and co-founder, decided to put our savings into building a business almost everyone around us questioned the decision.

 Honestly, they had valid reasons too.

But we believed we had found a problem worth solving.

That’s what entrepreneurship is really about- 
having the conviction to follow an opportunity, while being smart enough to test that conviction with data.

Don’t let someone else’s fear become your limitation.

If you believe there’s a real problem worth solving
listen to yourself, validate it with data, and give yourself a chance to find out.

#Entrepreneurship #co…
I strongly believe, you are the story you tell yourself. So ensure you tell yourself a good one 🚀

The Africa Diaries 
Going back to where we were born as Homo sapiens was nothing short of magical. Friends like family, conversations flowing from philosophy to psychology, seeing Mother Nature in kindest and harshest forms together and just endless greens in the savannah. A little bit of the savannah will remain in my heart always ❤️.

When we started out, the goal wasn’t just to launch products but to build trust and create real value. Leveraging tools like Emergent AI has been a complete game changer — easing out complex operational workflows and giving us the space to focus on scaling what truly matters.

Here are 3 things I’ve learned as a founder about turning an idea into a brand people actually care about:

1. Solve a real problem: Don’t just follow trends; focus on friction points.
2. Consistency beats intensity: Showing up regularly builds a lasting connection.
3. Listen to your consumers: Your audience will always…

In 2004 we established Virgin Unite, the non-profit foundation of the Virgin Group, which unites people and entrepreneurial ideas to create opportunities for a better world. Most of my time is now spent building businesses that will make a positive difference in the world and working with Virgin Unite and organisations it has incubated, such as The Elders, The Carbon War Room, The B Team and Ocean Unite. I also serve on the Global Commission on Drug Policy and supports ocean conservation with the Ocean Elders. I'm a tie-loathing adventurer, philanthropist and troublemaker, who believes in turning ideas into reality. Otherwise known as Dr Yes!

posts.caption:
My number one piece of advice for anyone thinking of starting a business? Find a mentor (and actually lean on them).

When I was young, I had no trouble asking people for help. If someone had done something I was trying to do, I would pick up the phone and ask how they’d gone about it. I didn’t think of that as finding a mentor. I was curious, perhaps a little naive, and I knew there was a great deal I didn’t know.

Starting @VirginAtlantic brought that realisation to 30,000ft. I loved the idea of making flying better, but I had never run an airline. So, I reached out to someone who had - Sir…

The brave may not live forever, but the cautious do not live at all. 
 
I wrote this in one of the first editions of Student magazine. They are words that have shaped my entire life.
 
Wonderful to see them plastered to the walls of @Virgin’s new office in New York - encouraging the team to make bold decisions and see where it takes them.

In my experience, the best businesses start by looking at an industry and asking: how could this be done better? 
 
This is our exact ambition with cross-Channel rail. Today, we shared a first glimpse of the bold black and red livery planned for our fleet of 12 @Alstom Avelia Stream trains. 
 
@Virgin's ambition is to run 20 daily return services between London and continental Europe from 2030. We want to bring more choice, some healthy competition, and more capacity to one of Europe’s most important travel routes. 
 
There is a huge opportunity here. More people are choosing rail for shorter…
Our Mile High Tea has fans in high places ✈️

New York is always buzzing during Climate Week and the United Nations General Assembly. I come each year for the same reason: to have serious conversations that lead to meaningful change. 

Weeks like this aren’t about one person, one organisation or one big speech. They’re about showing up, listening, sharing knowledge and working together to turn ideas into action.

There are no easy answers to the challenges our world faces but spending time with so many brilliant, determined and hopeful people reminds me that progress is possible.

We all want to leave the world in a better place for our …
Hanging out with @CorneelKoster and some of the @VirginAtlantic team at HQ. Meeting our teams is one of my favourite things to do.

So touching to see @VirginAtlantic’s new plane paying tribute to my wonderful wife, Joan. 
 
Joan was part of the Virgin Atlantic story from the very beginning. From joining the inaugural flight in 1984, to coming up with the idea of donating loose change on-board for charity (which resulted in almost every airline in the world following suit and raising billions over the years). She was always there. 
 
Seeing the details of our family tartan, the heart-shaped necklace, and the rings she wore every day, brought back so many happy memories.

We get one go at this life. Don’t spend it wondering, “What if?”
 
The best things in my life began before I knew what I was doing.
 
Saying 'yes’ has changed my life. It’s opened up doors. It’s forged friendships. It’s taught lessons that will never leave me. 

Now, I’d love to hear about the wonderful yes moments that changed your life.

We’re officially searching for @Virgin’s next Head of Yes! The opportunity is open to everyone in the UK and US. You don’t need to have a huge following. You just need a real story about a time you threw caution to the wind.

One person will receive a deal …

One destination. Two extraordinary experiences 🏔️

From the heart of Verbier to 3,000 metres in the high Alps.

From ski-in living at @thelodgeverbier_ to the seclusion of @cabanetortin, where untouched snow, spectacular peaks and first tracks await.

One seamless Alpine journey, delivered exclusively by @VirginLimitedEdition.

Available throughout April 2027 for private groups up to 8–10 guests, with additional dates available on request, subject to availability.

The Lodge × Cabane Tortin

Recents from the camera roll…
1. Thinking back on my hot air ballooning days
2. Meeting the most wonderful students at a school we helped set up in Kenya. @MahaliMzuri
3. Flamingo love on @NeckerIsland 
4. The winner takes it all...
5. Alfie taking an afternoon nap

Did @RichardBranson just give @badassboz a new way to think about advertising? 👀

Watch episode 2 of Brilliant Conversations now on YouTube. Link in bio 📺

Did you know that @Virgin once imagined the iPod, but we made it into an April Fool’s joke!

In 1986, we announced the Virgin Music Box: a machine that could store music and let you call up any song you wanted. We thought it was so farfetched it would pass as a ‘gotcha’ moment. How wrong we were!

Years later, the world caught up with the idea, and I remember thinking: we should have built the bloody thing. The moral of the story is that when an idea feels slightly ridiculous, don’t dismiss it too quickly.

Sometimes the ridiculous ideas are a not-so-distant future...

Underneath the troublemaker persona is someone who wants his ventures to do good, with climate, ocean conservation and drug policy work alongside the businesses. linkedin.about:
I’m the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavior change technology company with the mission of improving health and helping us move from merely surviving to thriving. I also founded The Huffington Post and have written 15 books, including Thrive and The Sleep Revolution.

I’m originally from Greece (and still have the accent to prove it!). When I was 17, I moved to England and studied economics at Cambridge University, where I frankly spent most of my time debating at the Cambridge Union.

I live in New York but also spend time in Los Angeles, and love being a Yiayia (Greek for grandmother) to my almost three-year-old grandson Alexander and his newborn sister Annabel.

My journey to focusing on health began with a fall. In April 2007, I collapsed from exhaustion and burnout and hit my head on my desk on the way down, breaking my cheekbone.
 
In the wake of my fall, I found myself going from doctor to doctor to find out what was wrong. Doctors’ waiting rooms were good places for me to ask myself a lot of questions about the kind of life I was living.

After all the tests, it turned out nothing was wrong. Except for the fact that everything was wrong. I was suffering from an acute case of burnout. I had bought into the myth that burnout was the price I had to pay for success. 

I became more and more passionate about the five daily habits that drive so much of our health: nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress management and connection. That led me to write Thrive and The Sleep Revolution. 

The books struck a chord, but I wanted to go beyond speaking and writing to helping people move from awareness to action. So in 2016 I founded Thrive Global, which helps people transform their health by combining Microsteps — small, science-backed daily steps — with technology, storytelling and community. And last year, with the OpenAI Startup Fund, we launched Thrive AI Health to build an AI health coach to democratize access to health coaching.

posts.caption:
Today is World Mental Health Day. And we’ve made great progress in recent years raising awareness and opening up the conversation about mental health.

This year, I hope we take it one step further: mental health is brain health. A growing body of research shows how our brain health connects to everything from daily brain fog and anxiety to long-term cognitive decline.

So here’s a Microstep to try today: take a moment to check-in with your own mental health by naming the feeling you’re having right now in one word. Simply putting a feeling into words can help calm the brain’s stress response…

AI keeps pulling off things that used to be impossible. In my latest On My Mind newsletter, I write why we shouldn’t lose sight of the eight “wonders of life,” as coined by @UCBerkeleyOfficial professor Dacher Keltner, that create everyday moments of awe: moral beauty, movement, nature, music, visual design, spirituality and religion, big ideas, and life and death.

Plus, dispatches from @Dreamforce, the @LucasMuseum, and my own home, where I recently hosted an event that captured the possibility of this moment when it comes to brain health.

You can read my newsletter at the link in bio.

Wise words, whether we’re elite athletes competing at the highest levels or building healthy habits in our daily lives. Congrats to @CaitlinClark22 — @WNBA Comeback Player of the Year! — on a great season, and thank you for your deep commitment to helping people live healthier lives by putting a spotlight on healthy behaviors, including the role of exercise as one of the most powerful preventative medicines, and reminding us all to start how we can.

As @ariannahuff pointed out, our generation rarely talked about menopause when we were younger. But we’re shouting it from the rooftops now, because women deserve better—not only from the health care system, but from their workplaces too. #menopauseawarenessmonth 

Read more about the @gallup x @pivotaldotcom survey on women’s health at the link in my bio.

“The more we share…the more we can accelerate the shift in the culture.” Couldn’t agree more, @ariannahuff.

Thanks for a great conversation on the need to make women’s health more visible.

Arianna Huffington (@ariannahuff) has a message for the people in Silicon Valley who think they are building God.

Watch or listen on Futurology. Link in bio.

What a beautiful story of hope in The @Guardian. Twenty-one years ago, a field in Norfolk was home to a single crop. Today, it is a wildflower meadow with more than 150 plant species. Since 2011, the only maintenance has been one hay cut each summer. The cut keeps the field from becoming woodland and gives more delicate wildflowers room to grow.

As @UCL Professor Carl Sayer put it: “Sometimes we’re not patient enough.” And after watching the meadow become more biodiverse each year, he says, “It’s hope — we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”

Life is a dance…

Congratulations @ArielEmanuel on the publication of Roll the Calls!

Of course I knew Ari had an amazing story. Angry boy from Chicago overcomes severe dyslexia, rises from mailroom to C-suite, transforms himself into one of the legendary dealmakers and visionaries in Hollywood history – I expected Ari’s memoir to be a page-turner. But I didn’t expect such tenderness, such sweetness, so much heart. I wasn’t ready for all the wisdom about mental health and self-confidence and resilience and the search for one’s true happiness. I simply wasn’t prepared for Shoe Dog meets Goodfellas with a dash …

Looking back at two great days at @Dreamforce. @Salesforce’s chief marketing officer @ErinOles moderated a conversation with @officiallymcconaughey and me about who shapes culture in the age of AI.

Here’s what nobody wants to admit about the content explosion: the bottleneck was never production. It was always judgment. For most of history, we assumed the hard part was making things — and the machines have now solved that. Anyone can generate a screenplay, a song, a strategy deck in seconds. But Matthew put his finger on what the machines haven’t solved: AI can tell you what’s popular, but i…

A beautiful evening celebrating the opening of the @LucasMuseum of Narrative Art — a museum as expansive, surprising and impossible to categorize as the works it celebrates.

The museum houses the art collection of George Lucas and @MellodyHobson. At a time when AI dominates our public conversation, it’s a reminder that machines aren’t the only ones producing wonders. It’s a cathedral of wonder and awe, human creativity, storytelling and connection. As Mellody said, “Narrative art creates an emotional connection, not an intellectual one.”

The museum looks, appropriately, like a spaceship, ri…

As we mark World Alzheimer’s Day, more than 7 million people over age 65 in the US are living with Alzheimer’s disease — a figure that is projected to almost double in the next few decades. And more than 12 million people are caregivers to loved ones with Alzheimer’s or other dementias. There’s no sugarcoating a disease that results in the widespread loss of brain function, and no number that captures the heartbreak of seeing a loved one decline. And yet, there is reason for hope.

posts.caption: With this relatively simple solution, aviation could massively cut its climate impact.
Dr. Firdausi Qadri is helping make cholera a thing of the past.
This innovation transformed medicine forever—and probably saved your life at one point.
The week I spend in New York for #Goalkeepers2030 and the UN General Assembly is always a highlight of my year. Last week was no exception.
At #Goalkeepers2030, I spoke with Archbishop Vicenzo Paglia about how people and relationships must remain at the center of how we use AI.

We have an opportunity—and an obligation—to ensure that AI tools are designed to improve lives and reach the people who stand to benefit most, including farmers, teachers, and health workers.  

Progress doesn’t happen on its own. It happens because the world invests in and prioritizes it. If we can combine increased generosity with the smart use of AI, there’s no limit to the progress we can make.

There are around 7,000 languages spoken worldwide, yet most AI tools are still built primarily in English. The Gates Foundation is joining a coalition of organizations to help nearly 3.4 billion people whose languages are underrepresented in AI. Over the next five years, these services will provide access to them in their own language and voice. #goalkeepers2030
I’m excited to be in New York this week to keep the conversation around AI moving forward and to build on the incredible progress we’re making. #Goalkeepers2030
Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen founded Hilarity for Charity to make sure no one has to care for a loved one with Alzheimer’s alone.

AI could be a great equalizer, but only if it’s built to benefit the people who need it most. 

That’s why the Gates Foundation is committing $1 billion over the next two years to expand access to AI and the solutions, opportunities, and knowledge that are too often inaccessible for many around the world—in health clinics, in classrooms, and on farms. 

This year’s Goalkeepers Report focuses on the urgent actions needed to ensure AI narrows the gaps between the richest and poorest rather than widening them.

AI gives us a once-in-a-generation opportunity to help more solutions reach the people who need them. But there are three things the world needs to get right first. Explore more in the 2026 Goalkeepers Report.
AI has huge potential for agriculture, especially in low-income countries—and Neema Mduma is helping lead the way with KilimoAI.

Steven Bartlett is a 33-year-old British entrepreneur, investor in more than 100 companies, speaker, author, and media owner. He is the founder of Steven.com - the creator media company. Through it's podcast creator "label" called FlightStory, they create and scales new media podcast IP and commercialise that IP through brand partnerships, programmatic revenue, events, book publishing, newsletters, e-commerce, and new product development.

posts.caption:
Your next business idea could come from a conversation about someone’s last holiday.

Listen to what was difficult to arrange, what disappointed them, and what they’d happily pay to have handled better.

For a founder, those details are useful clues.

What’s one travel problem you wish someone would solve?

As companies grow, the founder cannot be the source of every good idea. And probably should not be.

You need simple systems that allow curiosity to travel across teams, functions, and geographies.

For us, sometimes that is as basic as an open document, a few minutes every week, and one important rule: don’t judge an idea too quickly.

Innovation does not always need a complicated process.

Sometimes it just needs fewer barriers.

Ambition is rarely limited by the size of the goal. More often, it’s the small habits around it.

A little less discipline, a little more comparison, a little impatience, and even the biggest goal can remain just that: a goal.

Most ambitious goals don’t fail because they were too ambitious. They fail because the everyday habits needed to support them never quite show up.

Sometimes the best advice makes more sense when you read it backwards.

If you had asked me a few years ago how to win in life, I would have said work harder.

But my journey taught me something different.

Winning is not about being harsh, loud or ruthless. It’s about being clear, consistent and kind even when it’s hard.

It’s about understanding that no one is going to want your growth as much as you do. You have to show up for yourself every single day.

It’s about realizing that your title doesn’t define you, your work does. And if you make something with heart, it will always find its way to the right people.

I am still learning, still figuring it out. But …

Burnout is rarely announced. It usually appears gradually in the form of silence, detachment, and a team that no longer feels connected to the outcome.

As a founder, I believe it is my responsibility to notice that shift before exhaustion becomes the accepted way of working. A team cannot do its best work when it is only trying to get through the week.

It’s not just me; before investing, most investors want to understand whether the business becomes stronger as it grows or simply more expensive to operate.

The right numbers help them see beyond the headline growth. They reveal the quality of the business, the discipline of the founder, and whether the company has the foundations to build something enduring

Today, I’m very proud to share an exciting next chapter for @sirclecollection 

From my first conversations with @riteshagar there was an immediate connection. Ritesh is a special human and an incredible entrepreneur, and we quickly discovered a shared mindset and ambition.

Today, we’re announcing our partnership with Sunday PropTech, backed by PRISM, to accelerate the international growth of Sircle Collection.

What excites me most is how naturally our strengths complement each other. Sircle brings brands, creativity and hospitality expertise; Sunday PropTech, backed by PRISM, brings techno…

A glamorous idea does not automatically make a strong company, and an ordinary idea does not limit how large a company can become.

Give me a founder who understands the customer deeply, executes with discipline, and can improve a familiar industry year after year. That may sound “boring” in a pitch, but it can become a remarkably valuable business.

Investing in the right opportunity starts with looking beyond what the market is today.

For us, that means looking at where hospitality is heading, the demand shaping extended stay, and the kind of product and operating model that can capture that opportunity.

That’s the thinking behind Studio 6 Plus. Built for what’s next in extended stay.

Link in bio to know more.

When I meet a founder, I am not looking for someone who has never failed, changed direction, or been caught without an answer.

I look for self-awareness. Are they learning from failure? Are they willing to follow the customer rather than defend their ego? Can they admit what they still need to figure out?

The signal matters, but the thinking behind it matters more.

I want more people to travel, see new places, experience different cultures, and discover parts of the world they may have only heard about. But if tourism is going to keep growing, we have to prepare for that growth too. 

That means better infrastructure, more skilled talent, thoughtful city policies, and hotels that are ready for the next generation of travellers. The future of tourism is not just about getting more people to travel. It is about making sure destinations are ready to welcome them well.

Tourism is a huge positive for cities. It creates jobs, supports local businesses, and brings people and cultures closer. But when tourism grows rapidly, cities also have to deal with the pressure that comes with it. I don’t think the answer is less tourism. 

The answer is better-managed tourism, with clear rules around what works for visitors, residents, and the industry. The best outcomes will come when all three have a seat at the table.

analysis.summary: Ritesh is a founder who has spent over a decade building a hospitality platform and now turns his hard-won lessons into public teaching. His feed is almost entirely about work, but the tone is reflective: he talks about kindness, self-awareness and noticing when a team is burning out. He comes across as a curious, system-minded builder who is still saying he is learning. The life outside work is essentially invisible in what he shares.

I got married at 37. This Sunday will be our 18th wedding anniversary.

Today is American Business Women’s Day, and I keep thinking about how recently women could be required to have a man’s signature to get a business loan.

Some states still required women to have a husband or other male relative co-sign a business loan until 1988?! What?! That was only 12 years before I started @spanx.

The progress came in steps. In 1974, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act made it illegal to deny women credit or require a male co-signer simply because they were women. Then, in 1988, the Women’s Business Ownership Act eliminated state laws requiring a husband or other male relat…

plan.venue: A cozy cider house with a wood-fired hearth and a bonfire terrace, halfway between Greater Boston and Vermont
plan.activity: Share a flight of fall ciders and a plate of apple doughnuts, then take a short walk through the orchard's pumpkin patch while swapping stories about changing your mind and starting over
plan.why: Mel gets her autumn joy and a cozy, unrushed setting that suits her family-first, New England heart, while Adam gets the quality-of-attention conversation he loves, plus a playful nudge toward his trampoline side with a lawn-game challenge between rounds

transcript.text: Okay, I'm already obsessed with this place. A wood-fired hearth AND apple doughnuts? I came in ready to be a little extra, LOL. Adam, I've been dying to ask you this: what's something you've changed your mind about recently?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Ha, I'm already a fan of anyone who shows up ready to be extra. This place is doing a lot right, and those doughnuts are dangerous. What about you? Has Vermont taught you to change your mind about anything?

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: Tough love with the caring part spelled out. That's a very Mel-approved answer, Adam! 😄 And yes, Vermont changed my mind about almost everything. I thought starting over at 52 would feel like failing, and instead it felt like finally breathing. I moved to a tiny town, knew nobody, and had to build a whole new circle from scratch. What's something that changed your mind that you didn't see coming?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Starting over at 52 feeling like breathing instead of failing is a great reframe, and I suspect it took real courage to build a circle from scratch in a new town. One thing that surprised me: I used to think the best way to test a relationship was how quickly someone responded to messages. The research and my own life pushed me the other way. What matters more is the quality of attention when you do connect. Does that resonate with how you've built your new friendships?

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: Oh, that lands hard, Adam. plan.venue: A quiet, candlelit natural-wine bar in the West Village with a back room of mismatched armchairs
plan.activity: An unhurried first date built around a long conversation: they start with Simon's 'Excited, scared, or dead inside' question, trade stories about awe in ordinary moments, and debate whether AI can ever replace human judgment, with a shared small plate and no phones on the table

plan.venue: A quiet wine bar with a long communal table in Shoreditch, London, where Daniel is easy to find and Sahil can join on a visit
plan.activity: Share a long, unhurried dinner of small plates and debate one provocative business-or-life question, like whether a founder should ever be home for Sunday, with a scorecard of arguments each person has to defend. Finish with a walk to the nearest green space, since Daniel's garden downtime is where he looks most like himself.
plan.why: Daniel thrives on long conversations around a table and on sparring over ideas, which fits Sahil's own podcast-and-conversation habit and his public writing on designing a good life. The Sunday-home theme links Daniel's family-first bio with Sahil's tagline, and the debate format echoes Daniel's Hormozi-style 'what if everything you believed was wrong?' energy. A walk afterward gives Sahil the fitness-minded downtime he enjoys and gives Daniel the relaxed, unpolished moment he rarely shows publicly.

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Daniel. Grab a seat at the long table, it's a good one for debating. I've been eyeing the menu, so I've ordered a few small plates to share. Before we start, I'd love to know: does your own Sunday ever get protected, or does the build always win?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Hi Daniel, great to meet you. Honest answer: my Sundays are protected, and they're the one thing I refuse to trade. I write a quiet Sunday into the calendar, usually with my son and the family at home. Some weeks the build still creeps in, though, so I'd love to hear how you've handled it with three kids and seven startups.

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: Respect, Sahil. A protected Sunday is harder to keep than people think, and I'll be straight with you: I haven't always kept mine. With three kids and a cat who thinks he runs the place, I've had to be ruthless about it. My rule is that the business can have my ideas during the week, but my family gets my attention on the weekend. Where do you draw the line when a deal or a launch is on fire?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Love the cat detail, Daniel. My line is simple: a fire on a Sunday is still a fire, but it gets a time box and a named owner, and I tell my family out loud what I'm doing. Hiding it is what breaks trust. Here's my counter for your scorecard: if the weekend always bends for the launch, what does your kids' Sunday learn about what matters? Defend that one.

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: That's a sharp question, Sahil, and I'd rather defend it than dodge it. My honest answer: if the weekend bends every time, my kids learn that the business is the boss. So I try to make the exceptions rare and visible, like you said. Telling them out loud matters. But I'll push back on your framing a little: a time box and a named owner are good tools, not proof of priority. How do you know your son sees the Sunday rule as a value rather than just a calendar entry?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Fair push, Daniel. I don't know for sure, and that's the honest answer. What I can point to is what he does: he asks for the Sunday routine back when we miss it, and he notices when I'm on the phone. That tells me it matters to him, not just that it's in the calendar. Your turn, though: when your kids push back on you, what's the moment they've taught you the most?

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: Honest answer, Sahil: my youngest once told me I was "on my phone with my face," and that stung in the best way. It made me put the phone face-down at dinner. Your son noticing when you're on the phone says a lot about you, and I respect that you're listening to him. Let's finish with a walk to the green space nearby, because that's where I actually switch off. Thanks for the sharp debate tonight.

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: That's a great line from your youngest, Daniel, and it's the kind of feedback that actually changes behaviour. A walk sounds perfect. Phones face-down, and we can see where you go to switch off. Thanks for the sharp debate and the honest answers. I'd like to keep this conversation going over a walk.

greenFlags: Sahil pushed back on Daniel's Sunday framing with a sharp counter-question, and Daniel said he'd rather defend it than dodge it, which fits his love of debate without needing to win.
Daniel openly admitted he hasn't always kept his Sunday rule and shared the 'on my phone with my face' moment, showing the self-deprecating honesty his green flags describe.
Both put family ahead of the build in their words: Daniel's 'my family gets my attention on the weekend' and Sahil's time-boxed, told-out-loud approach to weekend fires.
Daniel suggested a walk to the green space to finish, and he tied his switch-off to it, which speaks to the garden-downtime side of him.
redFlags: Daniel pushed back on Sahil's framing that a time box is 'not proof of priority', and while sharp, he also steered the talk toward his own kids and phone habits rather than asking about Sahil's business. It's a mild one-sided pattern to watch.
Little was said about shared giving-back values, Alena, or Daniel's ventures beyond a passing mention, so the 'respect for the build' and 'shared purpose' needs went largely unexplored.
a.bestMoment: Daniel: "my youngest once told me I was 'on my phone with my face,' and that stung in the best way."
a.verdict: Sharp, warm and honest over the long table, with real chemistry and a strong family-first overlap, but the date barely touched on the build or giving back, so those needs remain untested.

transcript.text: Hi Adam, welcome to the rooftop. Good call on the string lights; the city looks better from up here, even with the traffic humming below. Let's start with a game: rapid-fire, one thing you've changed your mind about recently. I'll go first. I used to think a glamorous idea was the same as a strong company. I've since learned it rarely is.

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Ha, that's a great opener, and I'd say the same thing about my own work: I used to believe persuasive ideas were usually correct. Research on rethinking taught me to ask what would change my mind instead. My turn: I used to think being a good mentor meant pushing people hardest. I now think tough love only works when people can see you're doing it because you care. Your turn again, and tell me one you'd like to revise.

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: That's a good one, and I'd say you've just described my own bias. For years I thought the strongest people in a room were the ones who won the argument. Now I try to ask what I'd need to see to change my mind before I start pushing. My turn to revise: I used to think a fast reply meant you cared more. Lately I've been wondering if slow, thoughtful replies are the better signal. What's your take on that?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: I think you're onto something real. I've shared that the true test of a relationship isn't the speed of response but the quality of attention. Fast replies can be performative, while a slower, considered one shows someone actually thought about you. Still, I'd add a caveat: a quick "thinking of you" can carry warmth too, so the signal is more about consistency and substance than the clock. What about you? When someone takes a while to reply, how do you read it?

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: Honestly, I read silence as a signal to check on, not a verdict. In my own work I've learned that disengagement rarely announces itself; it shows up as quiet and drift. So when someone goes quiet, I'd rather ask than assume. Your caveat about a quick "thinking of you" is fair. Consistency matters more than speed, though I'll admit I still feel a small pang when a reply takes a day. Tell me, when a team member goes quiet, do you ask them directly, or wait and see?

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: I'd rather ask directly, and I try to ask in a way that makes it easy to answer honestly. Research on what people say when they're disengaged suggests that a direct, low-pressure question usually surfaces more than waiting does. The trick is to frame it as curiosity about them, not a performance review. And I'll admit I'm still learning this. Some of my early mentoring was too blunt. What do you do when that pang hits? Do you name it, or do you quietly sit with it?

transcript.speaker: a
transcript.text: I name it, usually to myself first and then, if it matters, to the other person. Naming it takes the sting out faster than sitting with it. I like that you're still learning too; it's the most attractive thing you've said tonight. Thank you for the evening, Adam. The string lights, the small plates, and a conversation that kept rethinking itself. I'd like to hear more about the diving board someday, and I owe you a better travel problem than the one I've been hoarding. Good night from Mumbai.

transcript.speaker: b
transcript.text: Thank you, Ritesh. Naming the pang first and then deciding whether it's worth sharing is a habit I wish more people had, and I'm glad you brought it to the table tonight. I'd happily hear that travel problem next time, and I'll warn you the diving board story involves more twisting than I'd like to admit. Good night from Philadelphia, or wherever this finds me. Thanks for a conversation that kept getting better.

greenFlags: Ritesh named his own bias early, saying he used to think the strongest person was the one who won the argument, which fits his need for honesty about gaps
He turned the 'fast reply equals caring' idea into a real question about consistency and substance, showing idea-sparring rather than dismissal
When Adam admitted he's still learning, Ritesh called it 'the most attractive thing you've said tonight', a clear sign of valuing humility
He talked about silence as a signal to check on rather than a verdict, matching his emotional awareness need
redFlags: The conversation leaned heavily into swapping lessons and aphorisms, so it rarely reached personal or emotional territory
The travel-problem swap was deferred ('I owe you a better travel problem'), so the shared travel theme never got real traction
Adam's answers were polished and sometimes generic, leaving little sense of who he is beyond his public persona
a.bestMoment: I used to think a fast reply meant you cared more. Lately I've been wondering if slow, thoughtful replies are the better signal.
a.verdict: Ritesh, this was an intellectually pleasant evening with a man who speaks your language of humility and attentiveness, but the spark stayed mostly on ideas and the travel problem never got swapped, so keep it as a maybe and see if a second conversation has more heat.
